summary: SkillComposer lets non-programmers program a simulated caregiving robot (RCareWorld) in natural language. A coder LLM emits JSON function-call programs over five primitives, an evaluator LLM plus a static schema validator gate each program (up to five revisions), and accepted programs are compressed by the Stitch library-learning algorithm into macros that an LLM documents and adds to the schema. It is evaluated with a 2x2 ablation (40 prompts x 5 runs) and a 12-person within-subjects study. The LLMs used are never named. The paper is about end-user robot programming, not software development.

claims.evidence: Table I: Coder+Eval beats Coder alone in 5 of 6 prompt categories (e.g. multi-step HRI 0.02 -> 0.98, goal planning 0.08 -> 0.68), at roughly 4-5x generation time. Success is judged by simulator outcome over 5 runs with SDs.

Table I contradicts this: Coder+Stitch matches or trails Coder alone (goal planning 0.00 vs 0.08), and full SkillComposer trails Coder+Eval on spatial reasoning (0.40 vs 0.76). The authors concede macro learning 'primarily affected program complexity rather than success rate'.

claims.claim: SkillComposer improves usability and reduces user effort versus a baseline coding LLM
claims.evidence: Table II: fewer prompts on all three tasks, higher success on 1 of 3 tasks, lower on feeding (0.67 vs 0.75). SUS 72.1 vs 61.4 (d=0.46), but paired t-tests p>0.05 on every subjective metric; 11/12 preferred it. The baseline also lacks the evaluator loop, so effects cannot be attributed to macros.

claims.claim: Macro use grows as more prompts are processed
claims.evidence: Fig. 5 only, descriptive, 20 prompts per environment.

patterns.note: An evaluator LLM before execution vs no evaluator wins on simulated success in 5/6 categories, at 4-5x latency. The only comparison is against no verification at all; there is no simulator-feedback (execution) baseline, and the domain is robot JSON programs.
An online library of learned macros shortens programs but does not raise success alone or with the evaluator (Table I).
All learned macros go into every prompt's schema (not on demand). The authors expect degradation as the library grows and suggest retrieval as future work.

methodology.sample: 40 natural-language prompts (20 Objects, 20 Feeding) x 4 variants x 5 runs; user study with 12 non-programmers, 3 tasks per system, within-subjects, counterbalanced
methodology.baselines: Coder-only LLM (ablation and user study); no execution-feedback or prior robot-programming system
methodology.models: Not named anywhere in the paper (coder, evaluator and documentation LLMs)
methodology.variance: Mean +/- SD over 5 runs; user study paired t-tests, all p>0.05
methodology.languages: JSON function-call robot programs in a Unity/Python simulator

standards.peer_review: Submitted to IEEE Humanoids 2026; not peer-reviewed
standards.artifacts: None released (no code, prompts, or model identity)

biases.detail: Simulated tabletop and feeding tasks over five primitives.
No artifacts and the LLMs are unnamed, so nothing can be reproduced.
Abstract says learned abstractions improve success and usability; Table I and the non-significant tests do not support this.
User-study baseline has no verification at all, conflating the evaluator effect with the macro effect.

verdict_reason: Off-topic: natural-language robot programming for non-programmers in simulation, not software development with LLM agents or its human side. The abstract's headline (learned abstractions improve success and usability) is not supported by its own Table I or by its non-significant user-study tests, and the models are never named.
applicability: Does not transfer to a backend Java team's discovery or onboarding harness. The only faint echo: in this toy domain, auto-mined skill libraries shortened outputs without improving success. That is a reason not to assume automatically learned skills help unless measured.
